name: Adzera (Retired)
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.note: Retired bookkeeping languoid (2008 split of Adzera [adz]/Sukurum/Sarasira); no languoid-specific description — covered under adze1240.

new_statements.quote: Stress in Amari is not phonemic. In general, the first syllable of a two-syllable word is stressed, and in words of more than two syllables, the first syllable is stressed, and then every alternate syllable is stressed. Slightly heavier stress falls on the first syllable. e.g. sàgat woman; ì-saŋʔ is enough; màmu cassowary; màragàmp white; bìŋan-gàŋʔ my name; gàdugàdu type of banana; Bùsuŋàwa woman's name; ŋàrubìni good
new_statements.citation: Holzknecht, Susanne. 1986. A morphology and grammar of Adzera (Amari dialect), Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea. In D. C. Laycock et al. (eds), Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 24 (Pacific Linguistics A-70), 77-166. Canberra: Research School of Pacific Studies, ANU. DOI 10.15144/PL-A70.77.
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (90 pp., pdfinfo title "A morphology and grammar of Adzera (Amari dialect), Morobe Province, Papua New Guinea", author Susanne Holzknecht). Rendered PDF page 18 (printed p. 94) to PNG and read it: section "2.5 Stress" reads exactly "Stress in Amari is not phonemic. In general, the first syllable of a two-syllable word is stressed, and in words of more than two syllables, the first syllable is stressed, and then every alternate syllable is stressed. Slightly heavier stress falls on the first syllable." followed by the eight examples with grave marks on the initial and every alternate syllable (sàgat, ì-saŋʔ, màmu, màragàmp, bìŋan-gàŋʔ, gàdugàdu, Bùsuŋàwa, ŋàrubìni) — matches the repor…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive stress; main stress on the first syllable of the word, with rhythmic stress on every second syllable after it (syllables 1, 3, 5...), the first being slightly stronger than the others. Left-to-right trochaic alternation from the left edge; no weight sensitivity mentioned.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: in words of more than two syllables every alternate syllable after the first is stressed, the first syllable carrying slightly heavier stress (examples màragàmp, gàdugàdu, ŋàrubìni, Bùsuŋàwa).
new_statements.exceptions: None listed; the rule is hedged only by 'In general'. Stress marks in the examples fall on the first syllable even when it is a prefix (ì-saŋʔ 'is enough') and on odd syllables across a suffix boundary (bìŋan-gàŋʔ 'my name').
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (grammatical word including affixes), citation forms in isolation; intonation is treated separately in sec. 2.6 (declarative falling; question rising then sharply falling on the last syllable).
new_statements.identity_note: adze1241 is a Glottolog bookkeeping languoid for the retired ISO code azr (retired 2008-01-14, CR 2007-186), which was split into Adzera [adz] = adze1240, Sukurum [zsu] and Sarasira [zsa]. The quoted statement describes the Amari dialect of Adzera and belongs to adze1240; under the census-counting law (retired codes confer no identity) it should be filed under adze1240 and adze1241 closed as a duplicate, not entered as a second language. No opened source gives a stress statement for Sukurum or Sarasira.

sources.note: No stress statement for Adzera, Sukurum or Sarasira (phoneme tables, dialect-distinguishing features only). Only mentions: speakers perceive dialect differences as 'intonation, stress, or speed of delivery' (ch. 4 intro); an 'unstressed position' vowel-reduction note under another Markham language (p. 57); a comparative remark on 'stress rules' in Watut reflexes.
